nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What have studies indicated about the level of MP contamination in mangrove ecosystems?
nodes.answer: Studies have indicated that mangrove ecosystems have substantially higher MP contamination compared to other ecosystems.
nodes.paragraph: Rivers, surface runoff, and sewage systems indirectly transport MPs, influencing mangrove ecosystems (Mehmood et al. 2023). Wind-driven deposition on beaches and proxim- ity to waste disposal sites also play a significant role in the deposition of MPs in coastal areas (Riaz et al. 2024). Mangrove ecosystems have been found to have substan- tially higher MP contamination as compared to other eco - systems (Liu et al. 2022). Plastic presence in mangrove eco- systems constitutes a significant portion of overall marine debris, as evidenced by recent studies (Browne et al. 2007; Li et al. 2021). Regardless, most studies focus on plastic waste (Browne et al. 2007), while studies on MPs in man- groves are still in their infancy. Previous research found that the mangrove sediment had a higher concentration of MPs compared to the marine sediment in the Beibu Gulf, China. That means the difference was substantially high: 264 2 items/kg in mangrove sediment compared to 0 11 1 items/ kg in marine sediments (Jiao et al. 2021).

nodes.question: How does environmental pollution specifically impact mangroves?
nodes.answer: Environmental pollution, particularly solid waste like floating single-use plastic bags, can obstruct water flow and damage the roots and branches of mangroves, leading to stunted growth or death.
nodes.paragraph: Despite these obstacles, there has been a notable rise in mangrove cover within the Indus Delta. Likewise, Fig. 1 Mangrove cover sites in Pakistan Environmental Science and Pollution Research mangrove marshes in Sindh and Baluchistan face several threats (Wood et al. 2013). These include deforestation due to urban development, changes in salinity levels caused by diverting freshwater, mixing of industrial effluents (Wood et al. 2013), depletion of fish stocks leading to damage to mangrove ecosystems, the decline of coral reefs affecting the forests in Baluchistan and Sindh, rising sea levels from climate change posing a significant threat, and the impact of water pollution on mangrove populations (Giri et al. 2015; Rafique 2018). Another risk is posed by environmental pollution. The presence of solid waste, such as the floating single-use plas - tic bags along the coastline, can have detrimental effects on the surrounding mangroves (Mukhtar and Hannan 2012). nodes.answer: The mixing of industrial effluents can harm mangrove populations by altering their natural habitat and health.

nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What impact does untreated sewage have on mangroves according to the paragraph?
nodes.answer: Untreated sewage hinders the propagation of mangroves and contributes to the acidification of local waters.
nodes.paragraph: 2021). Untreated sewage hinders the propagation of mangroves and can contribute to the acid- ification of local waters (Saher et al. 2019). The release of untreated waste into the ocean directly leads to an increase in ocean acidification (Weis 2024). As the largest city in Pakistan with a population of over 20 million, poor waste management practices have unfortunately turned Karachi S seashores into dumping grounds (Afzal et al. 2024). The absence of treatment plants for harmful substances, includ- ing microplastics (MPs), continuously resales the environ- ment, compromising mangrove ecosystem sustainability (Riaz et al. 2024). This work provides insight into the functions of man- groves in CO2 management and potential risks associated with water pollutants, particularly MPs. We also discussed the sources of MPs and their environmental and ecological implications for coastal and mangrove ecosystems. In sum- mary, this study highlights the need for effective research and the establishment of improved plastic waste manage- ment practices to reduce the release and introduction of MPs in mangrove ecosystems, especially in Pakistan. The manu- script emphasizes further research on behavior, accumula- tion, and the impact of MPs in these coastal and mangrove environments.

nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What are some stressors that have increased pressures on ecosystems over the past decades?
nodes.answer: Some stressors include chemical pollution, habitat destruction, climate change, and introduced harmful species.
nodes.paragraph: These ecosystem services depend on the good functioning of ecosystems, which in turn is the result of the rich interactions between species, as well as between species and their environments. Simply said, ecosystem functioning and the resulting ecosystem services depend primarily on biodiversity (Hooper et al. 2005; Le Provost et al. 2023). The differ - ent health concepts EcoHealth, OneHealth, and Planetary Health (Lerner and Berg 2017), all suggest that biodiversity loss will lead to a degradation in ecosystem services which in turn will lead to increased health risks for humans, livestock, and wildlife (Schmeller et al. 2020). Pressures on ecosystems from stressors such as chemical pollution, habitat destruction, climate change, and introduced harmful species have constantly increased over the past decades. The series of Scientists Warnings all outline the consequences of those pres- sures on the global life-support system (Cavicchioli et al. 2019; Ripple et al. 2017; 2021; Schmeller et al. 2022). Some studies reported on the effects of water pollution on human health and well-being.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What types of ecosystems have been notably affected by anthropogenic forcings according to the paragraph?
nodes.answer: Coastal ecosystems have been notably affected by anthropogenic forcings.
nodes.paragraph: In contrast, the populations of G. barbata have remained stable in Eastern Provence and Corsica. The main possible causes of decline are uprooting, overgrazing by herbivores, habitat destruction and competition with introduced seaweeds. The relevance of ecological restoration of G. barbata populations was assessed. Keywords Conservation, Cystoseira complex, Fucales, Gongolaria Barbata , Mediterranean Sea, Change over time, Disturbances The Anthropocene1 3 (but see4) represents a new era in which anthropogenic forcings have profoundly modified ecosystem functioning, to such an extent that they constitute the main forcing. The effects of global change are evident in the structure, dynamics, functioning and resilience of marine and terrestrial ecosystems5 13. The cumulative impacts of the increase in direct and indirect anthropogenic forcings have a particularly pronounced effect on coastal ecosystems (e.g. habitat destruction, eutrophication, contamination, overfishing, invasive species, global warming, extreme events and modification of trophic networks). The various stresses act over time (short-term and/or long-term disturbances) in an additive and synergistic way on species, populations, ecosystems and their capacity to provide ecosystem goods and services (e.g6,7,14 16).

nodes.question: What challenges do contaminated sediments in river deltas pose?
nodes.answer: Contaminated sediments in river deltas pose risks for the open sea and related management challenges due to pollution and sediment stability issues.
